paragraphs: A winning lottery ticket is a sparse part of a neural network that retains accuracy close to the original dense model. This paper investigates whether the connectivity of these subnetworks helps explain their performance. The central question is how a network can lose many connections while still allowing information to pass effectively through its layers.

The authors represent each feedforward layer as a bipartite graph and examine its spectral properties. They focus on the Ramanujan property, associated with graphs that remain strongly connected despite being sparse. Their analysis uses Cheeger’s inequality for irregular graphs to connect spectral characteristics with connectivity.

Empirically, winning tickets retain this property even at substantial sparsity. Accuracy and resistance to noise begin to decline when many layers lose it. These observations motivate pruning layers individually while preserving their Ramanujan property. The resulting strategy improves existing pruning algorithms in the reported experiments, supporting connectivity preservation as a useful practical guide rather than establishing a universal accuracy guarantee.
icml-2022-a-study-on-the-ramanujan-graph.tldr: Preserving a spectral connectivity property during pruning empirically helps sparse neural networks retain accuracy and robustness.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can differ in which graph structures they can distinguish. This paper compares extensions designed to exceed the expressive power associated with the Weisfeiler–Leman test. Its focus is the structural information these architectures can represent, making expressiveness itself the object of study.

The comparison covers four approaches: higher-order Weisfeiler–Leman methods, preprocessing small substructures, preprocessing neighborhoods within a small radius, and slightly perturbing a graph before computing its representation. The authors first improve the perturbation-based approach and prove that the change strictly increases that variant’s expressive power.

The main comparisons use carefully constructed examples that one extension can distinguish while another cannot. Such examples make differences between approaches concrete without requiring a single ranking to capture every capability. The paper also provides difficult examples for each extension and proves results about counting cliques and cycles. Together, these findings clarify which structural distinctions different design choices can capture and where their expressive limits remain.
icml-2022-a-theoretical-comparison-of-gr.tldr: The paper proves differences in the structural distinctions several powerful graph neural network extensions can express.

paragraphs: Tensorial convolutional neural networks use tensor decompositions to reduce parameter counts or improve generalization. However, their structure creates problems even before training begins: standard Xavier and Kaiming initialization often produce unsuitable starting weights. Initialization rules tailored to one decomposition also do not readily transfer to another, making architecture exploration harder.

The paper proposes a common initialization framework that generalizes Xavier and Kaiming methods across tensorial architectures. Its first step is a Reproducing Transformation, which expresses the backward computation as an equivalent convolution process. This places forward signal propagation and backward gradient propagation within a shared mathematical treatment.

Using the convolution operators in both directions, the framework controls the variance of features and gradients and derives fan-in and fan-out initialization rules for different tensorial networks. The authors demonstrate more stable training, faster convergence, and improved results. The contribution is therefore both a practical way to choose starting weights and a unified basis for handling architectures that previously needed separate initialization approaches.
icml-2022-a-unified-weight-initializatio.tldr: A unified initialization framework controls signal and gradient variance across tensorial convolutional networks, improving their reported training behavior.

paragraphs: Adding random noise to gradient descent can improve how a learned model performs beyond its training data. Usually, the perturbations at different steps are uncorrelated. This paper asks whether the relationship between consecutive perturbations is itself an important design choice, rather than treating independent noise as the default answer.

The proposed method, Anti-PGD, uses anticorrelated perturbations across successive optimization steps. In plain language, consecutive noise contributions tend to oppose one another. Across a variety of objective functions studied in the paper, this method generalizes substantially better than ordinary gradient descent and gradient descent with uncorrelated perturbations.

The authors also provide theoretical analysis supporting these experiments. In the settings analyzed, Anti-PGD reaches wider minima while the comparison methods remain in inferior regions or diverge. This links the temporal structure of injected noise to where optimization ends up. The result suggests a useful direction for training-method design, while the stated experimental and theoretical findings concern the objectives and settings examined.
icml-2022-anticorrelated-noise-injection.tldr: Anticorrelating noise across gradient steps improves generalization on the studied objectives, with theory connecting the method to wider minima.

paragraphs: Combining multiple neural-network predictions can improve uncertainty estimates and robustness, but reliable Bayesian neural-network predictions may require many evaluations. This paper explores a cheaper complementary operation inside convolutional networks: combining nearby locations in their feature maps. The authors implement this spatial smoothing by inserting a few blur layers.

Experiments show improvements in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and robustness across a range of ensemble sizes. With smoothing, Bayesian networks achieve strong predictive performance using only a handful of ensemble members. The method also improves conventional deterministic networks, so its reported usefulness extends beyond models that explicitly combine multiple predictions.

The authors present evidence suggesting that steadier feature maps and a smoother loss landscape help explain these gains. They also interpret global average pooling, pre-activation, and ReLU6 as special cases of spatial smoothing, offering a common explanation for their benefits. The broader contribution is an empirical and conceptual connection between local feature averaging and advantages usually associated with ensembles.
icml-2022-blurs-behave-like-ensembles-sp.tldr: Adding blur layers to convolutional networks empirically improves accuracy, uncertainty estimates, and robustness through spatial feature smoothing.

paragraphs: Searching over discrete choices is difficult when evaluating each candidate requires access to a black-box function and valid choices must satisfy combinatorial constraints. Model-based optimization adds another challenge: each search step requires optimizing an acquisition function that selects what to evaluate next. Heuristic solvers approximate this inner problem and can be awkward to adapt to constraints.

NN+MILP combines a piecewise-linear neural network, used as a surrogate for the expensive function, with mixed-integer linear programming to optimize the acquisition function. MILP supplies a flexible way to state domain-specific constraints and provides optimality guarantees for the acquisition problem. Those guarantees concern candidate selection within the model-based procedure.

The authors test constrained and unconstrained tasks involving DNA binding, binary quadratic optimization, and neural architecture search. Their framework matches or exceeds specialized black-box algorithms in these experiments. Acquisition optimization takes a few minutes with standard software and hardware, showing that a general constrained solver can be practically useful in the reported settings.
icml-2022-constrained-discrete-black-box.tldr: NN+MILP combines neural surrogates with mixed-integer programming to select discrete candidates while handling combinatorial constraints.

paragraphs: A model can encounter inputs during deployment that differ from its training data. Test-time adaptation addresses this by updating the model as those inputs arrive. The paper identifies two problems with existing approaches: updating on every sample is expensive, and adaptation to unfamiliar data can reduce performance on data resembling the original training distribution.

EATA addresses the computational problem through a sample-efficient entropy-minimization objective. It excludes uninformative samples from backward computation, reducing the number of costly updates. The authors report that this selection also improves accuracy on shifted data, so the efficiency gain accompanies a predictive benefit in their experiments.

A second objective discourages changes to weights that are important to the existing model. These weights tend to be preserved during adaptation, helping alleviate forgetting while other updates accommodate the new inputs. Experiments on CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R support the combined method. Its contribution is to treat adaptation efficiency and retention of earlier capabilities as connected requirements of deployment-time learning.
icml-2022-efficient-test-time-model-adap.tldr: EATA selectively updates on informative test samples and protects important weights to improve adaptation efficiency while reducing forgetting.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel is built from derivatives describing how a neural network’s outputs change with its parameters. It is useful for studying training and generalization. Although some infinitely wide networks permit analytical kernel calculations, practical finite networks require computations that can be prohibitively expensive in both time and memory.

This paper analyzes those computational and memory requirements in depth. Using the internal structure of neural networks, the authors develop two algorithms that change the exponents governing these costs. The improvement therefore concerns how resource requirements scale with problem size, making finite-width kernel calculations substantially more efficient.

The methods apply as black-box procedures to differentiable functions, including neural networks, and are released in the Neural Tangents package. More efficient computation supports uses already associated with finite-width kernels, including initialization, comparisons of model conditioning, architecture search, and meta-learning. The paper’s central contribution is computational infrastructure that makes this analytical tool more practical to use on finite models.
icml-2022-fast-finite-width-neural-tange.tldr: Two algorithms improve the scaling of time and memory costs for computing finite-width neural tangent kernels.

paragraphs: When approximating a matrix using a subset of its columns, some columns are more useful than others. Leverage scores help identify useful choices by relating columns to spaces defined by leading singular vectors. This paper broadens that relationship so the selected singular vectors can come from an arbitrary subset.

The authors establish a precise geometric connection between these generalized scores and principal angles, which describe how subspaces align. This connects a chosen collection of columns with a chosen collection of singular vectors. It provides a mathematical basis for reasoning about column selection beyond the usual focus on leading directions.

The paper uses this relationship to design approximation algorithms with provable guarantees for generalized column subset selection and sparse canonical correlation analysis. Numerical experiments provide further insight into the methods. The resulting bounds strengthen the theoretical understanding of matrix approximation, while the geometric connection offers a potential building block for additional algorithms involving the selection and comparison of subspaces.
icml-2022-generalized-leverage-scores-ge.tldr: Generalized leverage scores connect matrix-column selection to subspace geometry and yield approximation algorithms with provable guarantees.

paragraphs: Decision trees remain strong tools for supervised learning on tabular data, while generative adversarial networks have been especially successful on images. This paper develops generative trees to bring useful elements of tree-based prediction into tabular data generation. It connects the choice of training loss, model structure, and boosting-based learning.

The analysis starts from proper supervised losses, for which the Bayes rule is optimal. This leads to an adversarial loss formulation that is tight when the discriminator satisfies a calibration property naturally met by decision trees. Under common assumptions on the supervised loss, the generator can use a shared chi-squared loss across the considered formulations.

The authors introduce an adversarial training algorithm compatible with boosting and a second approach called copycat training. In copycat training, the generator copies the discriminator’s tree structure during execution and completes it for the hardest discrimination task, with a boosting-compatible convergence result. Experiments examine real-versus-generated discrimination and missing-data imputation, connecting the theoretical construction to practical tabular tasks.
icml-2022-generative-trees-adversarial-a.tldr: Generative trees adapt decision-tree losses, structures, and boosting to tabular generation through adversarial and copycat training.

paragraphs: When an agent cannot directly observe the full state of its environment, past observations can help it decide what to do. Learning a useful representation of that history can consume substantial experience. This paper proposes using an already trained language transformer as a frozen memory module for reinforcement learning.

The technical bridge is FrozenHopfield, which associates observations with the transformer’s pretrained token embeddings. A modern Hopfield network stores those embeddings. Observations pass through a random projection that remains fixed, and the resulting queries retrieve embeddings from this store. This makes observations usable by the language transformer without training the transformer itself.

The full method, HELM, incorporates this history representation into actor-critic architectures. Because the representation of past experience does not have to be learned from scratch, the authors report substantially better sample efficiency than competitors. HELM also achieves state-of-the-art results on Minigrid and Procgen. The findings support reusing pretrained sequence-processing capabilities as a source of memory for partially observable control.
icml-2022-history-compression-via-langua.tldr: HELM uses a frozen language transformer to represent observation histories, improving sample efficiency in partially observable reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Symmetry-aware models can share what they learn across examples related by transformations. Their use becomes difficult when the effect of a transformation on the input is hard to describe. For instance, a useful symmetry may exist even though its action on an image is not available in a convenient mathematical form.

The paper introduces symmetric embedding networks, or SENs, to bridge that gap. An SEN maps inputs into a feature space where transformations have a known action. It trains jointly with an equivariant task network, allowing the combined system to learn a representation with explicit symmetry while handling the more complicated input space.

The authors test this approach in transition models using three distinct forms of symmetry. Their experiments show that SENs make equivariant networks applicable to data with complex symmetry representations. They also find that the approach can improve accuracy and generalization relative to fully equivariant and non-equivariant alternatives. The contribution is a learned interface between difficult input transformations and structured models that can exploit symmetry.
icml-2022-learning-symmetric-embeddings-.tldr: Symmetric embedding networks learn feature spaces with known transformation rules, enabling equivariant models to handle more complex inputs.

paragraphs: Hidden Networks find useful subnetworks inside a randomly weighted neural network by learning which connections to retain. The learned connectivity pattern is called a supermask. This paper identifies a training problem: the supermask can stop improving even when gradients remain nonzero, leaving available learning information underused.

The proposed solution overlays multiple hierarchical supermasks for the same task, producing a multicoated supermask. This extends the connectivity representation available to the method. The authors report that using several masks increases accuracy without additional training cost, addressing the observed stagnation while retaining the hidden-network approach.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show a better balance between accuracy and model size. In the highlighted result, a ResNet-101 with seven coats outperforms its Hidden Networks counterpart by a reported 4%. It also matches the accuracy of a dense ResNet-50 while being an order of magnitude smaller. These findings show that a richer mask structure can improve the usefulness of subnetworks found within random weights.
icml-2022-multicoated-supermasks-enhance.tldr: Layering hierarchical supermasks improves the reported accuracy–size tradeoff of subnetworks selected from randomly weighted networks.

paragraphs: A mixture of linear regressions contains several component predictors, making the meaning of a single prediction error unclear. This paper defines prediction as returning a list with one value from each component. Its loss is the smallest loss among those component predictions, giving a concrete objective for evaluating the mixture.

Under this definition, a solution to empirical risk minimization has a small probability of prediction error. Finding such a solution is computationally difficult, however. The authors move beyond the usual realizable setting, where data are assumed to have been generated by a mixture of noisy linear models, and instead study fitting a dataset without that assumption.

They show that a version of expectation maximization finds the best-fitting lines under regularity conditions on the data and starting points. They also provide an algorithm whose runtime is polynomial in the number of data points and that approximates the best-fitting lines. An experimental comparison accompanies these results, connecting the prediction formulation to algorithms for fitting mixtures.
icml-2022-on-learning-mixture-of-linear-.tldr: The paper defines list-based prediction for regression mixtures and develops fitting guarantees beyond mixture-generated data, subject to stated conditions.

paragraphs: A molecule-generation system can propose structures with attractive properties yet fail to provide molecules that can be synthesized. This paper addresses that problem while also trying to preserve important structural motifs of a target molecule. Its goal is to generate useful chemical relatives with defined routes for making them.

The proposed variational autoencoder is conditioned on structure and incorporates reaction information. Its latent representation jointly encodes molecular structures and their reaction routes. A new sampling method measures structural similarity using information about those routes, so the search for related molecules accounts for both molecular form and synthetic paths.

The authors report generating molecules similar in structure and properties to seed molecules from both within and outside the model’s domain, with well-defined reaction paths. They also demonstrate molecules with higher activity than their seeds by concentrating the search on an important region of chemical space. The approach connects structural preservation, property-oriented exploration, and synthetic accessibility within one generative framework.
icml-2022-path-aware-and-structure-prese.tldr: A reaction-aware variational autoencoder generates molecules resembling target structures while providing defined synthetic routes.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from previously collected data. Conservative methods have been successful in this setting, but this paper finds that transferring them directly to multiple interacting agents can work poorly. In the reported experiments, performance deteriorates substantially as the number of agents increases.

The authors identify a difficulty in optimizing the value function: its non-concave shape makes policy-gradient updates vulnerable to local optima. Multiple agents amplify this problem because one agent’s poor policy can disrupt coordination across the group. Improving individual policies is therefore closely tied to achieving useful collective behavior.

OMAR, or Offline Multi-Agent RL with Actor Rectification, combines first-order policy gradients with zeroth-order optimization, which does not rely on gradients. The combination aims to optimize actors more effectively against conservative value functions. OMAR achieves state-of-the-art results across a variety of multi-agent control tasks in the paper. The findings support actor optimization as a practical intervention for the observed degradation of conservative offline learning in multi-agent settings.
icml-2022-plan-better-amid-conservatism-.tldr: OMAR combines gradient-based and gradient-free actor optimization to improve conservative offline reinforcement learning with multiple agents.

paragraphs: Communities in a graph can overlap: their boundaries may include both connections between groups and vertices shared by multiple groups. Ordinary edge-based partitioning does not fully capture this structure. This paper develops methods for hybrid partitions that account for both kinds of boundary, motivated by community detection and similarity-graph clustering.

The authors introduce two objectives extending conductance, a familiar measure of cluster separation, to hybrid vertex-and-edge boundaries. They then extend the cut-matching framework to obtain almost-linear-time algorithms with logarithmic approximation guarantees for both objectives. The guarantees connect computational efficiency with a quantified bound on solution quality.

The contribution also includes a working implementation that produces hybrid partitions and optimality certificates. It scales to graphs containing tens of millions of edges and is evaluated against competitive alternatives on real datasets. This practical component matters because the paper addresses a gap between fast methods for edge boundaries and much less developed methods for overlapping or vertex-based boundaries.
icml-2022-practical-almost-linear-time-a.tldr: New hybrid clustering objectives support almost-linear-time approximation algorithms that handle shared vertices and scale to very large graphs.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness is often presented as requiring a sacrifice in ordinary predictive accuracy. This paper examines whether part of that tension may originate in how robust error is defined. The authors argue that a conventional definition can encourage excessive local invariance, pushing a model toward too much smoothness.

They propose local equivariance as a better description of desired behavior: responses should change appropriately with nearby input changes. This leads to SCORE, a revised robust-error definition designed to make robustness and accuracy compatible while retaining worst-case optimization. The authors describe efficient minimization by replacing KL divergence with variants of distance metrics.

Their models achieve top-ranked performance on RobustBench under AutoAttack in the reported evaluation. SCORE also provides insights into overfitting and semantic input gradients in robust models. The paper’s claim is that the objective’s definition can help reconcile robustness and accuracy; its account of the origin of the tradeoff is explicitly a possible explanation, supported by the proposed formulation and experiments.
icml-2022-robustness-and-accuracy-could-.tldr: SCORE revises robust error around local equivariance, offering a way to reconcile accuracy with worst-case robustness.

paragraphs: Gaussian Markov random fields define probabilistic models using the sparse relationships in a graph. Deep versions add a multilayer structure, but the earlier framework was designed for lattice graphs. This paper extends that approach to general graphs, broadening the range of structured data it can represent.

The key contribution is a new layer designed for scalability. It supports efficient training through variational inference and can use existing graph neural-network software frameworks. This combines the probabilistic structure of a Gaussian field with a layered model that can operate on large graphs.

When the observation likelihood is Gaussian, the method permits nearly exact Bayesian inference for the latent field. Predictions can therefore come with uncertainty estimates, an explicit benefit of the probabilistic formulation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets compare favorably with both Bayesian and deep-learning alternatives. The result is a more broadly applicable Deep GMRF framework whose scalability and uncertainty capabilities are considered together.
icml-2022-scalable-deep-gaussian-markov-.tldr: A new Deep GMRF layer extends scalable probabilistic modeling to general graphs, with nearly exact latent inference under Gaussian likelihoods.

paragraphs: Control policies that act from images are often trained with visual representations learned from scratch in their deployment environments. This paper revisits whether representations pretrained on large computer-vision datasets can provide an effective starting point. The question is whether visual knowledge acquired elsewhere can support learning to act.

The authors evaluate this idea across Habitat, DeepMind Control, Adroit, and Franka Kitchen. They examine representation-training methods, data augmentation, and feature hierarchies to understand which aspects of visual pretraining matter. This makes the study a comparison of representation choices across diverse control domains.

The reported results show that pretrained visual representations can compete with, and sometimes outperform, ground-truth state representations when training control policies. The visual pretraining uses standard vision datasets without deployment-environment data. That distinction concerns the source of the visual representation: the paper studies how those externally learned features support subsequent policy learning. Its findings establish that useful visual information for control can transfer across this substantial difference in data source.
icml-2022-the-unsurprising-effectiveness.tldr: Visual representations pretrained outside deployment environments can match or exceed ground-truth state representations for learning control policies.

paragraphs: Fluent storytelling requires keeping track of the entities mentioned throughout a narrative. This paper studies whether large pretrained language models maintain that information coherently and consistently over long stretches of generated text. It introduces automatic measures of entity usage and uses them to quantify shortcomings in existing models.

To address those shortcomings, the authors add a dynamic entity memory to a pretrained language model. The system is trained end to end, with an auxiliary entity-related objective guiding what the model writes to memory and what it retrieves. This makes entity information an explicit part of the generation process.

Both automatic evaluation and human judgment show improved entity coherence with the memory mechanism. It is especially helpful for preserving entity information when the model’s context window is limited. The proposed automatic measures also correlate with human ratings and indicate story quality. The paper therefore contributes both a way to assess long-range entity handling and a memory-based method for improving it.
icml-2022-towards-coherent-and-consisten.tldr: A dynamic entity memory improves consistency in generated stories, while new automatic metrics track human judgments of entity coherence.

paragraphs: Predicting how sequence changes affect protein fitness can support variant analysis and protein design. Models trained on aligned related sequences have been successful, but their performance depends on having sufficiently large and diverse alignments. Some protein families are difficult to align, restricting where those methods work well.

Tranception combines an autoregressive transformer with retrieval of homologous sequences at prediction time. This brings sequence-model predictions together with information from related proteins. The authors report state-of-the-art fitness prediction, stronger performance on variants containing multiple mutations, robustness when alignments are shallow, and the ability to score insertions and deletions.

These capabilities broaden the range of variants and protein families the approach can address. The paper also introduces ProteinGym, a collection of assays measuring variant effects that increases both the number and diversity of evaluations relative to existing benchmarks. Together, the model and benchmark advance the prediction method and the breadth of evidence used to assess protein-fitness models.
icml-2022-tranception-protein-fitness-pr.tldr: Tranception combines autoregressive protein modeling with inference-time retrieval to improve fitness prediction across a broader range of variants.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning often builds representations using transformed versions of the same data. For time series, choosing suitable transformations can be difficult, particularly in industrial or medical applications. Domain experts may already have useful features for these signals, creating another source of guidance for representation learning.

The paper introduces ExpCLR, which uses expert features in place of the transformations commonly used by earlier contrastive methods. The authors first propose two desirable properties for time-series representations and show that existing approaches do not ensure them. They then construct an objective that uses expert features to encourage both properties in the learned representation.

Evaluations on three real-world time-series datasets show ExpCLR outperforming several state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised and semi-supervised representation learning. The findings support incorporating available domain knowledge directly into the learning objective. The approach matters because it offers a route to useful representations when meaningful transformations are elusive, while making expert-designed signal descriptions part of the learning process.
icml-2022-utilizing-expert-features-for-.tldr: ExpCLR uses expert features to guide contrastive time-series learning and outperforms several existing methods on three real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Evaluating causal inference is difficult because the outcomes a unit would experience under alternative treatments are not all observed. Observational treatment assignment can also be confounded. Researchers often compare methods on simulated data, but simplified simulations may poorly represent the particular dataset they need to analyze.

Credence uses a deep generative model to create synthetic data anchored to the observed sample’s empirical distribution. Users specify the form and magnitude of causal effects and confounding bias as functions of covariates. This combines data resembling the real sample with known causal quantities, making estimation errors measurable under the specified scenarios.

The framework evaluates how different causal estimators might perform on data similar to the observed sample. An extensive simulation study and applications using Lalonde and Project STAR data demonstrate its ability to assess relative method performance accurately. Its contribution is a way to make validation more relevant to the data at hand while retaining the controlled ground truth needed to compare estimators.
icml-2022-validating-causal-inference-me.tldr: Credence generates realistic synthetic data with specified causal effects and confounding to evaluate estimators for a particular observed dataset.

paragraphs: Choosing a pretrained model and fine-tuning settings can be expensive when a new dataset comes with a small compute budget. Repeated experimentation is also a concern for small datasets. This paper proposes learning how to make those choices from experience collected across many previous datasets.

The method trains a surrogate model using performance measurements from many deep-learning pipelines. Each pipeline includes a pretrained model and fine-tuning hyperparameters. A pairwise ranking objective teaches the surrogate which pipelines are preferable. For a new dataset, selection requires only simple descriptive features, such as image resolution or the number of classes.

The zero-shot aspect concerns selecting the pipeline from those dataset descriptions; the selected pipeline still includes fine-tuning. Under the strict time budget of the ChaLearn AutoDL vision benchmark, the approach clearly outperforms all challenge contenders. The result supports transferring knowledge about pipeline performance across datasets as a practical way to make model-selection decisions when extensive new experimentation is costly.
icml-2022-zero-shot-automl-with-pretrain.tldr: A meta-learned ranking model selects pretrained models and fine-tuning settings using only simple descriptions of a new dataset.
